fact_sheet.business_description: United Technologies Corporation (UTC) is a conglomerate comprising Pratt & Whitney (engines), aerospace systems, Otis (elevators), and climate/control businesses including Carrier [D01]. The company is currently managing the integration of the Rockwell Collins acquisition alongside the geared-turbofan engine ramp [D01, D07].
segments_and_separable_assets: Otis: 19.9% group sales share, 14.8% segment margin, 8.3% YoY sales growth [D06]
Climate, Controls & Security: 28.7% group sales share, 13.5% segment margin, 12.4% YoY sales growth [D06]
Pratt & Whitney: 28.4% group sales share, 9.5% segment margin, 15.2% YoY sales growth [D06]
UTC Aerospace Systems: 25.0% group sales share, 15.4% segment margin, 5.7% YoY sales growth [D06]
economics_vs_peers: Aerospace peers cited include Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, and General Dynamics [D04].
Elevator service should be benchmarked against Kone and Schindler; climate products against focused HVAC companies [D06].
Reported aftermarket growth indicates a recurring-revenue engine, but segment performance is offset by new-platform losses and divergent cyclicality [D06].

gate1.edge_statement: Third Point can apply its constructivist framework to separate UTC's distinct, high-value aerospace and elevator businesses, unlocking a conglomerate discount that the market is currently obscuring due to integration execution fears.
gate1.one_line_verdict: a multi-industry conglomerate with high-quality separable units that can be unlocked through a disciplined separation process.

gate2.variant_view: The market believes that UTC's conglomerate structure is necessary for managing the complex Rockwell Collins integration and offsetting cyclically weak segments like Otis new-equipment orders [D05]. We disagree, viewing the company as a collection of high-quality, distinct assets that are suppressed by an archaic conglomerate structure [D01, D05]. A formal separation into independent aerospace and elevator businesses will eliminate the holdco discount and allow these units to be valued in line with their respective pure-play peers [D05].
evidence: Conglomerate structure creates a sum-of-the-parts discount that is not reflected in the current EV/EBITDA of 11.0x [D04, D05].
High-quality units like Otis and Aerospace businesses are distinct enough to operate independently [D01].
Separation allows for better capital allocation and focus compared to the current integration-heavy corporate strategy [D05, D07].

final.memo:
United Technologies Corporation is a classic conglomerate that currently obscures the true value of its world-class aerospace and elevator assets behind an opaque corporate structure [D01]. At a current price of $120.15 and an EV/EBITDA multiple of 11.0x, the market is severely mispricing the underlying businesses by failing to account for the potential for independent valuation [D04, D05].

Our sum-of-the-parts analysis, benchmarking segments against pure-plays like Kone, Schindler, and top-tier aerospace firms, indicates an implied equity value of $144-$160 per share [D04, D06]. While the market frets over the Rockwell Collins integration and cyclicality in Otis, it ignores the high recurring revenue profile of these businesses and their clear path to margin expansion [D05, D06].

We intend to engage privately with CEO Gregory Hayes and the Board to advocate for a formal strategic review and portfolio separation [D01, D05]. Our asks are clear: separate the aerospace and elevator units to eliminate the conglomerate discount and set margin targets that force operational accountability against industry-leading peers [D06]. We believe the large, index-heavy register will be highly receptive to a clear plan for unlocking this value [D01].

We size this as a 5% position, reflecting our confidence in the 3:1 skew and the hard floor provided by the company’s strong FCF generation [D04, D06]. We will maintain this position as long as management engages constructively on the separation process, but we are prepared to take our case to the public if the Board remains anchored to its current strategy [D01, D05].
